analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices with manufacturers, ending the current ban on doing so.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; after introduction in January 2019 and one subcommittee hearing in September 2019, it died in committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law explicitly forbids the government from negotiating prices for drugs covered by Medicare's prescription drug benefit. This bill strikes that ban and directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with drug manufacturers on behalf of Medicare beneficiaries, starting with plan year 2020. Plans could still negotiate even lower prices, and formulary rules would not change. The bill was referred to two committees and never reached the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly tens of millions of prescription drug beneficiaries, who pay premiums and out-of-pocket costs tied to Part D drug prices; taxpayers, who help fund Part D, would also benefit if negotiated prices lowered federal drug spending. Independent pharmacies and plan sponsors would face lower input costs.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the current-law 'noninterference' provision that prohibits the government from negotiating Part D drug prices, and requires the Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with manufacturers for covered Part D drugs.
Requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations conducted and the prices and discounts achieved, creating public visibility into the results.
Lets plans still seek discounts below the negotiated price, so beneficiaries could see savings beyond the negotiated floor.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the legal guarantee that the government cannot negotiate Part D prices, potentially reducing their revenue on Medicare-covered drugs. Critics of Medicare negotiation have long argued that lower drug revenue could reduce manufacturers' investment in developing new drugs.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires negotiation but leaves the Part D plan structure and formulary rules in place and does not specify enforcement tools if manufacturers refuse to negotiate, so the savings achieved would depend entirely on the Secretary's bargaining position.

A standard objection to Medicare drug price negotiation is that lower revenue for brand-name manufacturers could mean less investment in new drug development; the bill contains no independent assessment of that trade-off.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside for seniors and taxpayers is large, since Medicare covers an enormous share of brand-name drug spending and other countries with government negotiation pay systematically lower prices. The main honest cost is the risk of somewhat slower development of future drugs if manufacturer revenue falls, and the bill's vagueness about enforcement means the savings are not guaranteed. The stronger design weakness is procedural: the bill never advanced far enough to be amended or tested, so no hearing scrutiny refined it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees for its entire two-year life; the only action beyond referral was a single subcommittee hearing in September 2019, and it never came to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, with 11 original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and in each case to the Subcommittee on Health.
The Subcommittee on Health held a hearing on September 25, 2019 — the only recorded action beyond referral.
The bill gathered 37 cosponsors, including one Republican, but was never reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: the legal prohibition on Medicare negotiating drug prices remains in place, and their Medicare drug revenue was untouched. No committee or member recorded a vote against the bill, so it died through inaction rather than open opposition.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 original cosponsors from both parties.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, held a single subcommittee hearing, and never brought it to a committee vote in two years.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and took no recorded action on it for two years.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against allowing the government to negotiate Medicare drug prices, arguing it would amount to price-setting and reduce investment in new medicines.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (36 of 37 cosponsors) but included one Republican, and no party ever went on record for or against the bill because neither chamber voted.

industries.note: The bill would end the current-law ban on Medicare negotiating Part D drug prices, directly threatening revenue on drugs sold to Medicare beneficiaries. Their pricing power over one of the largest drug purchasers in the world is what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Part D plan sponsors (health insurers offering prescription drug and Medicare Advantage plans)
industries.note: Negotiated prices, discounts, and rebates would lower the input costs plans pay for covered drugs, potentially reducing premiums and beneficiary out-of-pocket costs. The bill preserves plans' ability to negotiate even lower prices themselves.
